newsitem.title: ITALY: Advertisers urge EU help to scrap restrictive laws.
newsitem.headline: Advertisers urge EU help to scrap restrictive laws.

text.p: Advertisers called on the European Commission on Thursday for help in overturning legal restrictions on advertising in some parts of the European Union, saying they were an obstacle to a free market within the bloc.

Albert Winninghoff, president of the European Association of Advertising Agencies, told an industry conference that the laws, in France, Greece and Sweden, should be scrapped and the Commission needed to encourage Europe-wide deregulation.
"Products and services that are legally produced, legally distributed and legally consumed cannot be denied access to the power of legal communication," Winninghoff said.
Tobacco and alcohol advertising is strictly limited in France. Toy advertising and advertising to children in Greece and Sweden is not allowed.

Winninghoff also urged the EU's executive body to step in to tackle a three-year old law in France designed to stamp out corrupt business practices that has hurt advertising agencies' profits, saying that unless it did, other countries might follow suit.

That law, the so-called Loi Sapin, banned payment of unofficial commissions to ad agencies by media groups that sell advertising space on television or in the press. The money was charged to the clients placing the ads without their knowledge.
One client, himself a former advertising executive, condemned the old system as illegal "black money".

But Winninghoff said the law was hurting French agencies' competitiveness. "Conceived as a method of achieving transparency, the Loi Sapin has proved to be the worst method because of its anti-competitive effects," he said.

"The European Commission should intervene to restore the competitive viability of French agencies and to prevent the possible spread of revenue-reducing legislation to other parts of the EU," he said. He did not say how this should be done.
Greece and the Netherlands were considering similar restrictions on agency revenues, he added.
The Commission published a green paper, or consultation document, on commercial communications in May and the industry has until the end of October to submit written answers.
Paul Waterschoot, a senior official from the Commission's internal market division, said the aim was to make the current system more transparent and avoid unnecessary intervention.
But he agreed urgent action was needed to create a full internal market and prevent European advertising being shut out or left behind as new technology opens up a global market.
The Commission proposes setting up a committee to address general issues such as children's advertising or the regulation of sponsorship. He did not refer to the Loi Sapin directly.
"It's objective would not be to single out one or other member state's laws but rather to discuss how mutual recognition could be achieved," Waterschoot said.
He said such an approach would be better than a general EU directive (law) limiting itself to vague principles and open to different interpretations across the 15-nation bloc.

Winninghoff told the conference, the EAAA's annual meeting of advertising and trade bodies from 24 countries, that "antiquated statutory regulations" should be swept away to allow the cross-border brand building the industry now demands.
"Europe's advertising industry sees no role for legislation," he said. "Deregulation will do away with some very harmful laws that currently damage the interests of advertisers, media and agencies."
